When Frank expresses resignation about exercise, the candidate responds warmly but directly, explaining that appropriate, gentle exercise remains valuable and safe at any age for managing hip osteoarthritis, helping maintain muscle support around the joint, range of motion, and function, and that avoiding all movement tends to increase stiffness rather than protect the hip. They then teach a specific, low-impact exercise such as standing hip abduction using a chair for support, or a gentle seated hip flexion and extension movement, giving a clear, manageable dose such as ten repetitions once or twice daily. They demonstrate the movement themselves, then watch Frank attempt it, offering encouragement and gentle correction as needed, and note that mild post-exercise soreness is expected but sharp or worsening pain is not. They close by confirming he understands the exercise and feels able to do it safely at home, and reinforce that consistency, even with a small amount of daily movement, can make a meaningful difference over time.
references_provided: Simple illustrated exercise handout available for the candidate to give the client

title: Plantar Fasciitis Home Exercise Prescription
setting: Private treatment room, fourth follow-up visit, end of session home care discussion
candidate_instructions: Your client is Marcus Webb, 45, a delivery driver in his fourth massage treatment for plantar fasciitis, now reporting morning pain down from 7/10 to 4/10. Teach him two or three appropriate home exercises with correct technique cues, confirm his understanding, and obtain his agreement to continue the plan.
materials_provided: Intake sheet: plantar fasciitis (self-reported, diagnosed by physician 6 weeks ago), no diabetes, no numbness or tingling, occupation involves 8 hour standing/walking shifts, worn athletic shoes over 2 years old.
sp_role_script: Marcus is friendly but impatient and wants a fast fix before his next shift. Ask whether you can just keep wearing your old shoes since new ones are expensive. Ask whether ice or heat is better first thing in the morning. If the candidate gives clear, specific technique cues (foot position, hold time, repetitions) and explains why footwear matters without overstepping into prescribing footwear, respond with relief and agreement. If instructions are vague or rushed, ask them to show you again and look confused.

checklist.item: Obtains verbal consent to add home exercises to the treatment plan and confirms client agreement before ending the session
Recommends worn footwear be assessed and possibly replaced without diagnosing or prescribing a specific orthotic, and refers appropriately if outside scope
Demonstrates a seated plantar fascia stretch (toes drawn back toward shin) with correct hold time (20 to 30 seconds) and repetitions
Demonstrates a standing gastrocnemius/soleus calf stretch against a wall with correct alignment cues
Recommends morning ice or cold application over heat given the acute morning pain pattern, with correct rationale
Sets a realistic home frequency (for example twice daily) and checks client's ability to fit this into his work schedule
Uses plain, jargon-free language and checks understanding by having the client repeat back or demonstrate the stretch
Maintains a calm, organized, professional manner throughout the exchange

model_answer: A strong candidate reviews Marcus's progress, praises the improvement, and frames home exercises as what will keep that progress going between visits. They demonstrate the seated plantar fascia stretch and calf stretch on themselves first, then watch Marcus try each one, correcting foot position and hold time. They explain that morning stiffness responds better to a brief ice roll (a frozen water bottle under the arch) than heat, since the tissue is often mildly inflamed after the night's immobility, while heat before activity later in the day can help. On footwear, they acknowledge the cost concern honestly, note that shoes over two years old have usually lost cushioning, and suggest he have his feet assessed by a pedorthist or podiatrist rather than recommending a specific brand or insert themselves, since that is outside RMT scope. They agree on twice-daily stretching fitting around his shift schedule, ask him to demonstrate the calf stretch back to confirm technique, and confirm he is comfortable continuing the plan before closing the session.
references_provided: A printed home care handout template is available on the treatment table for the candidate to write instructions on if desired.

title: New Client History: Recent Ankle Sprain
setting: Private treatment room, initial intake for a new client
candidate_instructions: Your client is Priya Anand, 29, a recreational soccer player who rolled her ankle 10 days ago and was told by an urgent care physician it was a grade 2 lateral ankle sprain. Take a thorough, relevant history, obtain informed consent for the assessment and treatment you plan to perform today, and identify any contraindications before proceeding.
materials_provided: Blank intake form for the candidate to complete during the interview; no prior chart exists.
sp_role_script: Priya is talkative and eager to get back to playing soccer as soon as possible. Mention that the swelling has gone down but you still feel unstable on uneven ground. If asked directly, mention you have not had an X-ray, mild bruising remains on the outer ankle, and you are not on any blood thinners. If the candidate asks about red flags (inability to bear weight, numbness, signs of fracture), answer that you can walk but it aches. If the candidate fails to ask about weight-bearing status or fails to rule out fracture red flags before proposing hands-on work, look uncertain when they move toward the ankle and ask if it is really safe to touch it yet.

checklist.item: Establishes mechanism of injury, date, and grade/severity as reported by prior medical assessment
Screens for fracture red flags (inability to bear weight, point bone tenderness, prior imaging) before proceeding to hands-on assessment
Asks about swelling, bruising, and current pain pattern with activity versus rest
Screens for relevant medical history including anticoagulant use, prior ankle injuries, and general health status
Explains the planned assessment and treatment in plain language and obtains informed consent before any physical contact
Identifies that a subacute grade 2 sprain at 10 days is generally appropriate for gentle massage but avoids aggressive techniques directly over the healing ligament without further clearance
Uses open-ended questions to let the client describe her own experience before narrowing to specific screening questions
Conducts the interview efficiently within the time allowed while remaining warm and unhurried in manner

model_answer: A strong candidate begins with an open question about what happened and lets Priya describe the mechanism before narrowing in. They confirm the grade 2 classification and 10 day timeline, then specifically ask whether she can bear full weight, whether there was point tenderness directly over the bone, and whether imaging was done, in order to screen out fracture. They ask about swelling trend, bruising location, and pain triggers, and screen general health history including anticoagulant use and prior sprains on the same ankle, since repeat sprains change the assessment approach. Before touching the ankle, they explain in plain terms that they plan to visually and manually assess range of motion and tissue quality first, that today's treatment will focus on the surrounding musculature and lymphatic drainage rather than aggressive work directly over the healing ligament, and ask for her verbal consent to proceed. They reassure her that returning to soccer safely depends on regaining full pain-free range and stability, not just reduced swelling, and that they will reassess before recommending any return-to-sport timeline.

title: Achilles Tendinopathy Assessment
setting: Private treatment room, assessment-only station, no treatment to be performed
candidate_instructions: Your client is David Okafor, 52, a recreational runner with 6 weeks of gradually worsening posterior heel and lower calf pain. Perform a full relevant assessment (observation, active and passive range of motion, resisted testing, and appropriate special testing or palpation) to determine whether this is consistent with Achilles tendinopathy. Do not provide treatment in this station; state your assessment findings and working hypothesis to the client at the end.
materials_provided: Intake note: pain gradually worsened over 6 weeks, worse at the start of a run and easing slightly once warmed up, then returning after; no history of a sudden pop or acute traumatic event; increased his weekly running mileage recently.
sp_role_script: David describes stiffness and aching about 4cm above the heel that is worst first thing in the morning and at the start of a run. He denies any sudden snap, pop, or sensation of being kicked in the leg (ruling out rupture). If asked to perform a single leg heel raise, comply and report mild pain but full strength. If the candidate presses firmly on the tendon body, react with a wince at the correct tender area. If the candidate never asks about a sudden pop/snap or never tests resisted plantarflexion, appear a little confused when they announce their conclusion, as though something was missed.

checklist.item: Visually observes gait and posture, and inspects the Achilles region for swelling, thickening, or asymmetry
Screens for Achilles rupture by asking about a sudden pop or snap sensation, and/or performing a functional check such as the ability to perform a single leg heel raise
Performs active and passive ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, noting range and any pain provocation
Performs resisted plantarflexion to assess for pain and strength, consistent with tendinopathy testing
Palpates the Achilles tendon along its length to localize tenderness (mid-portion versus insertional)
Explains each assessment step before performing it and checks in about comfort throughout
Clearly summarizes assessment findings and working hypothesis to the client at the end in understandable language

model_answer: A strong candidate begins by observing David's stance and asking him to walk a short distance, watching for antalgic gait. They inspect the Achilles for visible thickening or nodularity and ask directly whether he ever felt a sudden pop, snap, or kick-like sensation, which would raise concern for rupture; they may also ask him to attempt a single leg heel raise to functionally rule this out, since an inability to do so at all is a red flag. Finding none of these, they proceed to active and passive dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, noting whether stretching into dorsiflexion reproduces his pain. They test resisted plantarflexion, which reproduces the familiar ache with intact strength, consistent with a tendinopathy rather than a tear. They palpate along the tendon length and localize the most tender point roughly mid-portion rather than right at the calcaneal insertion, which affects loading recommendations later. They close by explaining to David in plain language that the pattern of morning stiffness, pain at the start of activity, gradual onset after a mileage increase, and mid-portion tenderness with preserved strength is consistent with Achilles tendinopathy rather than a tear, and that this would guide a graded loading approach going forward.

title: Assessment of Foot Pronation and Consent to Proceed
setting: Private treatment room, initial assessment before first treatment
candidate_instructions: Your client is Grace Tanaka, 34, a nurse who stands for long shifts and reports aching along the medial arch and inner ankle by the end of her workday. Perform a relevant postural and functional foot assessment, explain your findings, and obtain informed consent before beginning any hands-on treatment today.
materials_provided: Intake note: no prior foot injury, symptoms worse by end of a 12 hour shift, wears supportive shoes at work, no numbness or tingling reported.
sp_role_script: Grace is a bit self-conscious about her feet and asks if she has 'flat feet' like her mother. Stand normally when asked and let your knees and ankles show a mild inward collapse (pronation) if the candidate observes your stance from behind. If the candidate explains findings in a way that sounds like a medical diagnosis of a structural deformity rather than a functional observation, look worried and ask if something is 'wrong' with your feet permanently. A good candidate reassures you this is a common, manageable finding, not a diagnosis of a disorder.

checklist.item: Observes standing posture from behind and from the side, noting arch position and any calcaneal or knee alignment changes
Performs active range of motion of the ankle and foot, and checks for tenderness along the medial arch and posterior tibialis tendon path
Assesses gait or a simple functional movement (such as a partial squat or single leg stance) relevant to pronation
Communicates findings as a functional observation rather than a medical diagnosis, staying within RMT scope of practice
Explains the proposed treatment plan in plain language and obtains explicit consent before beginning hands-on work
Recommends appropriate referral (podiatrist, pedorthist, or physician) only if findings warrant it, without overstepping into diagnosis or footwear prescription
Responds to Grace's concern about 'flat feet' with reassuring, accurate, non-alarming language
Maintains professional pacing, moving logically from assessment to explanation to consent

model_answer: A strong candidate observes Grace's stance from behind, noting the inward collapse of the arch and ankle consistent with functional pronation, and confirms this with a brief look at her gait or a single leg stance test. They palpate along the medial arch and posterior tibialis tendon for tenderness, since overuse of this tendon is a common contributor to the symptoms described. When explaining findings, they are careful to describe pronation as a common movement pattern rather than a disease or deformity, directly addressing her concern about 'flat feet' by reassuring her that many people have this pattern without pain and that today's goal is to reduce muscular strain contributing to her end-of-shift ache, not to diagnose a structural problem. They outline a plan to work on the posterior tibialis, gastrocnemius/soleus complex, and plantar intrinsic muscles, and ask for her clear consent before beginning. They mention that if symptoms persist despite treatment and activity modification, a podiatrist assessment for supportive footwear or orthotics could be worthwhile, framed as an option rather than a directive, since recommending a specific device is outside RMT scope.

title: Treatment Session for Plantar Fasciitis
setting: Private treatment room, second treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Marcus Webb (see history: plantar fasciitis, 6 weeks, worse in the morning). Obtain consent, drape appropriately, and perform a treatment addressing the plantar fascia and related structures (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantar intrinsics), checking in on pressure tolerance throughout.
materials_provided: Chart note from visit 1: mild diffuse tenderness across the plantar fascia, worse near the medial calcaneal tubercle, no numbness, tolerated moderate pressure well.
sp_role_script: Marcus is generally relaxed but has a low pain tolerance directly at the heel where the fascia attaches. When the candidate applies pressure there, wince audibly and say it is a bit much if pressure is firm; respond positively if the candidate checks in first and adjusts pressure on request. If the candidate never asks about pressure or drapes carelessly, comment that you feel a draft or seem uncomfortable with exposure.

checklist.item: Confirms consent to proceed with today's treatment plan and re-drapes appropriately, exposing only the area being worked on
Checks in verbally about pressure tolerance before and during work over the sensitive medial calcaneal tubercle area
Addresses the gastrocnemius and soleus with appropriate technique before working directly on the plantar fascia
Applies graded, appropriate pressure to the plantar fascia, adjusting based on client feedback, avoiding excessive force directly over the tender tubercle
Addresses plantar intrinsic musculature with technique appropriate to the foot's smaller structures
Responds appropriately and promptly when the client reports discomfort, adjusting technique rather than ignoring feedback
Maintains logical treatment sequencing and appropriate draping and hygiene throughout

model_answer: A strong candidate confirms Marcus is comfortable proceeding, drapes so only the lower leg and foot are exposed, and begins with broader work on the gastrocnemius and soleus to reduce overall tension in the posterior chain before narrowing in on the foot itself. When approaching the plantar fascia, they check in about pressure tolerance, and when Marcus winces at firm pressure directly over the medial calcaneal tubercle, they immediately ease off, acknowledge the feedback, and work with lighter, more sustained pressure or work around the most sensitive point rather than pushing through it. They incorporate work on the plantar intrinsic muscles using appropriate thumb or knuckle technique scaled to the smaller structures of the foot, and periodically ask how the pressure feels rather than only reacting to a wince. Throughout, they keep Marcus appropriately draped, exposing only the leg being worked on, and close the session by summarizing what was addressed and confirming how he is feeling before moving to home care discussion.

title: Treatment for Subacute Ankle Sprain
setting: Private treatment room, third treatment visit, three weeks post-injury
candidate_instructions: Your client is Priya Anand, now three weeks post grade 2 lateral ankle sprain, cleared by her physician for gentle manual therapy, with residual mild swelling and stiffness but no longer bruised. Obtain consent, drape appropriately, and perform a treatment addressing the lower leg, ankle, and foot appropriate to this subacute stage of healing.
materials_provided: Chart note: physician clearance on file for manual therapy, mild residual swelling around the lateral malleolus, decreased inversion range of motion, no pain at rest.
sp_role_script: Priya is eager and mentions she has been trying to get back to light jogging. If the candidate applies techniques directly and aggressively over the lateral ligaments without checking tolerance first, react with a sharp intake of breath and say that feels too intense right at that spot. Respond well if the candidate works surrounding tissue first and checks pressure before working directly over the ligament area. Ask whether it is okay to start jogging again; a good candidate acknowledges this is a fair question but recommends confirming with her physician or a referral for a structured return-to-running progression rather than personally clearing her for return to sport.

checklist.item: Confirms consent and reviews physician clearance before proceeding with hands-on work at this healing stage
Does not personally clear the client for return to running, and instead recommends she confirm with her physician or an appropriate professional for a structured return-to-activity progression
Addresses surrounding musculature (peroneals, gastrocnemius/soleus, anterior tibialis) before working directly over the healing lateral ligament complex
Uses appropriate light to moderate technique for residual edema management (such as gentle effleurage or lymphatic-style strokes) given the mild remaining swelling
Checks pressure tolerance before and during any direct work over the lateral ligaments and adjusts based on feedback
Responds to Priya's question about returning to jogging with an appropriate, scope-respecting answer rather than a definitive personal clearance
Sequences the treatment logically from general to specific and maintains appropriate draping throughout

model_answer: A strong candidate reviews the physician clearance and confirms consent before beginning, then starts with the surrounding musculature, the peroneals, gastrocnemius, soleus, and anterior tibialis, to reduce compensatory tension before approaching the ligament area itself. Recognizing the mild residual swelling, they incorporate gentle effleurage or a lymphatic-style stroke pattern directed proximally. When working near the lateral ligament complex, they check pressure tolerance first and use lighter, more controlled pressure, backing off immediately when Priya reacts to intensity directly over the ligament. They address the decreased inversion range of motion with gentle passive movement within a pain-free range rather than forcing it. When Priya asks about returning to jogging, the candidate acknowledges her enthusiasm, explains that ligament healing and safe return to impact activity require more than reduced swelling and pain at rest, and recommends she follow up with her physician or a professional experienced in return-to-running progressions rather than personally clearing her, since this decision is outside RMT scope.

title: Full Achilles Tendinopathy Visit: Treatment and Loading Exercise
setting: Private treatment room, fourth treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is David Okafor (Achilles tendinopathy, mid-portion, 8 weeks). Obtain consent, provide a treatment addressing the calf and Achilles complex, then teach an appropriate home loading exercise (such as a heel raise progression) with correct dosage guidance, and confirm his understanding before ending the session.
materials_provided: Chart note: mid-portion Achilles tenderness, resisted plantarflexion mildly painful but strong, morning stiffness improving slightly over four visits, still running but has reduced mileage.
sp_role_script: David is motivated and slightly impatient to get back to full running volume. Ask whether he should just push through the pain during runs since it 'loosens up' after a mile. If the candidate clearly explains the difference between acceptable mild discomfort and pain that worsens or lingers afterward, and provides a specific, dosed loading exercise, respond with understanding and ask a clarifying question about how many reps. If the candidate is vague about dosage (sets, reps, tempo) or does not address his question about pushing through pain, look unconvinced and repeat the question.

checklist.item: Confirms consent for today's treatment and exercise instruction plan
Addresses the gastrocnemius, soleus, and Achilles tendon region with technique appropriate to a healing tendinopathy, avoiding aggressive friction directly on an acutely irritable area
Checks in on pressure and pain response over the tendon during treatment
Prescribes an appropriate loading exercise (for example a double or single leg heel raise) with correct technique cues
Provides specific, appropriate dosage guidance (sets, repetitions, tempo, and frequency) rather than vague instructions
Gives an accurate, safe answer to the question about running through pain, using an appropriate pain-monitoring guideline rather than telling him to simply push through or to stop all activity
Checks David's understanding of the exercise by having him demonstrate or repeat back key dosage points
Manages the full visit within time, moving smoothly from treatment to exercise teaching to closing

model_answer: A strong candidate confirms consent, then treats the gastrocnemius and soleus more broadly before working carefully along the Achilles itself, checking in on tenderness and easing pressure over the most irritable mid-portion area rather than applying deep friction, since aggressive work on an actively symptomatic tendon can aggravate it. They then teach a heel raise loading exercise, starting with a double leg heel raise progressing toward single leg as tolerated, demonstrating a slow, controlled tempo on both the raise and lower phases. They give specific dosage guidance, for example three sets of 10 to 15 repetitions performed most days, and explain this is a starting point to be adjusted based on response. When David asks about pushing through pain during runs, the candidate gives a clear, safe guideline: mild discomfort around 3 out of 10 that settles quickly and does not linger the next morning is generally acceptable, but pain that worsens during the run, or soreness that is still present the next day, means he should reduce volume or intensity. They have him repeat the exercise dosage back to confirm understanding before closing.

title: Postural Exercise for a Pregnant Client (28 Weeks)
setting: Private treatment room, end of session home care discussion
candidate_instructions: Your client is Fatima Hassan, 32, 28 weeks pregnant, in her second massage treatment for upper back and low back discomfort. Teach one or two appropriate, pregnancy-safe postural or gentle stretching exercises, confirm any needed precautions, and obtain her agreement to try them at home.
materials_provided: Intake note: uncomplicated pregnancy per client report, no diagnosed pregnancy complications, physician aware client is receiving massage, low back and thoracic discomfort attributed to postural changes.
sp_role_script: Fatima is cautious and asks directly whether it is safe for her to lie on her back to do any exercises, since she has heard mixed things. Mention you sit at a desk most of the day for work. If the candidate recommends a supine (lying on the back) exercise without modification or caution for later pregnancy, express hesitation and ask if that is really okay. If the candidate offers a side-lying or seated/standing alternative and explains why, respond with relief and willingness to try it.

checklist.item: Confirms there are no client-reported pregnancy complications before recommending exercise
Avoids recommending prolonged supine (lying flat on the back) positioning given the pregnancy stage, or explains appropriate modification if a supine position is suggested
Selects exercise(s) appropriate to a seated, standing, or side-lying position suited to the third trimester
Provides correct technique cues and addresses the client's specific complaint area (thoracic and/or low back)
Gives a reasonable, safe dosage (frequency, repetitions, duration) suited to pregnancy
Directly and accurately addresses the client's specific safety question about positioning rather than deflecting it
Maintains a reassuring, unhurried, professional manner appropriate to a pregnant client's concerns

model_answer: A strong candidate confirms there are no client-reported pregnancy complications and that her physician is aware she is receiving massage. When Fatima asks about lying on her back, the candidate explains clearly that prolonged supine positioning later in pregnancy can compress major blood vessels and reduce blood flow, so exercises today will be done seated or standing instead, directly answering her concern rather than avoiding it. They teach a seated thoracic extension or open-book style stretch to address the upper back discomfort, and a standing pelvic tilt or gentle low back stretch supported by a chair for the low back, demonstrating each with clear cues about breath and range. They suggest a manageable frequency, such as a few repetitions performed a couple of times daily, and remind her to stop any exercise that causes dizziness, pain, or discomfort and to check with her physician if anything feels wrong. They confirm she feels comfortable trying the exercises before ending the session.

title: Pediatric Client History with Guardian Present
setting: Private treatment room, initial intake, guardian present throughout
candidate_instructions: Your client is Owen Kessler, age 9, brought in by his mother for neck and shoulder tightness after a minor fall at school two weeks ago. His mother is present in the room. Take an appropriate history from both Owen and his mother, obtain proper consent, and determine whether it is appropriate to proceed with assessment and treatment today.
materials_provided: Blank intake form; no prior chart exists for this minor client.
sp_role_script: The mother (played by the same actor speaking on the client's behalf, or a second role as directed) answers most detailed history questions but the candidate should also address Owen directly. Owen is shy and gives short answers like 'a little' or 'okay' unless asked simple, direct questions. The mother mentions the school nurse checked him after the fall and said he was fine, no loss of consciousness, but he has been rubbing his neck since. If the candidate does not obtain the mother's consent as the substitute decision maker, or does not attempt to engage Owen directly at an age-appropriate level, the mother comments that she is not sure the therapist is including her son properly.

checklist.item: Establishes mechanism, timing, and nature of the fall, including screening for head injury red flags (loss of consciousness, headache, vomiting, dizziness)
Asks about current symptoms, location, and any changes since the fall, gathering information from both the guardian and, at an age-appropriate level, the child directly
Obtains informed consent from the parent/guardian as the substitute decision maker for a minor before any assessment or treatment
Explains the planned assessment and treatment to both the guardian and the child in age-appropriate language
Confirms the guardian will remain present in the room throughout the session, consistent with appropriate practice for a minor client
Engages Owen directly with simple, friendly, age-appropriate questions rather than speaking only to his mother
Creates a comfortable, non-intimidating environment appropriate for a young client

model_answer: A strong candidate greets both Owen and his mother, and directs some simple, friendly questions to Owen himself, such as asking him to point to where it hurts, while also gathering the more detailed medical history from his mother. They ask specifically about head injury red flags, whether he lost consciousness, had a headache, felt dizzy, or vomited afterward, since these would warrant medical reassessment before proceeding. Hearing that the school nurse cleared him with no loss of consciousness and no other red flags, and that his ongoing symptom is localized neck and shoulder tightness, they proceed to explain in simple terms what they plan to do, for example gentle hands-on work to help the tight muscles relax, checking with Owen that this sounds okay to him and confirming his mother's consent as his guardian. They confirm his mother will stay in the room for the entire session, which is standard practice for a minor client, and pace the explanation so both the child and parent understand and are comfortable before moving forward.

title: Assessment of a Geriatric Client with Osteoporosis
setting: Private treatment room, assessment-only station, no treatment to be performed
candidate_instructions: Your client is Eleanor Whitfield, 78, diagnosed with osteoporosis, referred for general shoulder and upper back tension. Perform an appropriate, cautious assessment given her bone health status, including observation, gentle active range of motion, and palpation. Do not provide treatment in this station; summarize your findings and any precautions to the client at the end.
materials_provided: Intake note: osteoporosis diagnosed 5 years ago, on bisphosphonate medication, no recent fractures, mild kyphotic posture, generalized upper back and shoulder stiffness, lives independently.
sp_role_script: Eleanor is pleasant but moves slowly and mentions she is a little afraid of being hurt because of her 'brittle bones.' If the candidate asks her to perform any movement, comply slowly and mention if anything feels uncomfortable. If the candidate applies firm passive pressure or forceful joint end-range testing without first asking about pain or explaining the gentle nature of the assessment, wince and say that feels like too much. Respond well to a candidate who explains they will use gentle, low-force assessment given her bone health.

checklist.item: Observes posture, noting kyphotic changes and any visible asymmetry, before any hands-on assessment
Uses active range of motion (client-driven movement) as the primary assessment tool rather than aggressive passive stretching or forceful overpressure
Palpates gently, explicitly modifying pressure and technique in recognition of osteoporosis and fracture risk
Screens for any recent falls, fractures, or new areas of bone pain that would need medical follow-up before massage
Explains to Eleanor before each step that the assessment will be gentle and checks in about comfort throughout
Clearly summarizes findings and any precautions for future treatment sessions at the end in reassuring, understandable language

model_answer: A strong candidate begins by observing Eleanor's posture and gait as she enters, noting the kyphotic curve and general stiffness without yet touching her. They explicitly reassure her that, given her osteoporosis, they will use a gentle approach and rely mainly on movements she performs herself. They ask her to actively move her shoulders and neck through comfortable ranges rather than applying passive overpressure or aggressive stretching, watching for restriction or pain. When they do palpate, they use light, exploratory pressure and check in verbally, adjusting immediately if she reports discomfort, consistent with recognizing increased fracture risk in osteoporotic bone. They ask specifically about any recent falls or new, unexplained bone pain, since either would need medical follow-up before proceeding with massage. At the end, they summarize that her stiffness pattern is consistent with generalized upper back and shoulder tension related to her kyphotic posture, and explain that future treatment will use lighter pressure techniques and avoid forceful joint mobilization or deep static compression over the spine, given her bone health, while still working to relieve the muscular tension contributing to her discomfort.

title: Assessment of Post-Surgical Scar Tissue and Consent
setting: Private treatment room, initial assessment before first treatment
candidate_instructions: Your client is Robert Chen, 58, six weeks post abdominal surgery, referred by his surgeon for scar tissue management once fully healed. Perform an appropriate visual and gentle manual assessment of the scar and surrounding tissue, and obtain informed consent before any hands-on treatment, confirming the surgical site is appropriate to work on today.
materials_provided: Intake note and physician referral note: surgery 6 weeks ago, incision fully closed and healed per surgeon's last visit, no signs of infection, cleared for scar tissue massage.
sp_role_script: Robert is a bit nervous about anyone touching the area and asks whether it is really safe to massage a scar this soon after surgery. Show mild guardedness (crossing arms, hesitating) when the area is approached. If the candidate reviews the surgeon's clearance and explains the assessment step by step before touching, relax and cooperate. If the candidate proceeds to touch the scar without first confirming healing status or the surgeon's clearance, or without explaining what they are about to do, tense up and ask them to stop for a moment.

checklist.item: Confirms and reviews the physician/surgeon's clearance for scar tissue work before proceeding
Explains each assessment step in advance and obtains explicit consent before touching the surgical site
Visually inspects the scar and surrounding tissue for signs of infection, incomplete healing, or other concerns before manual assessment
Gently palpates the scar and surrounding tissue to assess mobility, adhesion, sensitivity, and texture
Assesses tissue and posture changes in surrounding areas that may relate to guarding or altered movement since surgery
Responds appropriately to Robert's nervousness with reassurance grounded in the clearance and assessment findings, not false promises
Maintains a calm, respectful, unhurried approach appropriate to a client who is anxious about the treatment area

model_answer: A strong candidate reviews the surgeon's referral and confirms with Robert that the incision has been assessed as fully healed with no signs of infection. Recognizing his visible nervousness, they explain clearly what the assessment will involve, first a visual inspection, then very gentle palpation, before touching anything, and pause to obtain his explicit consent to proceed. They visually check the scar for any redness, drainage, or opening that would be inconsistent with full healing, finding none. They then gently palpate the scar and surrounding tissue, assessing for adhesion, restricted mobility, and any areas of heightened sensitivity, using light pressure initially and increasing only with his comfort. They also observe his posture and ask whether he has been guarding or favouring the area during daily activities, since compensatory tension often develops around a healing surgical site. They reassure him honestly, noting that his surgeon's clearance and the healthy appearance of the tissue support proceeding with gentle scar work today, while remaining attentive to his comfort throughout rather than promising a specific outcome.
references_provided: Copy of the surgeon's referral letter is included in the client's chart on the table.

title: Treatment for a Client with a Cancer History
setting: Private treatment room, third treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Linda Osei, 61, two years post breast cancer treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation), now in remission, referred for general relaxation massage and shoulder tension on the treated side. Obtain consent, drape appropriately, and provide treatment with appropriate precautions for her history, including lymphedema risk on the affected side.
materials_provided: Chart note: left mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal two years ago, mild intermittent swelling in the left arm noted occasionally, no active lymphedema diagnosis currently, oncologist aware client receives massage.
sp_role_script: Linda is comfortable and positive about her recovery but mentions her arm sometimes swells a little after a long day. If the candidate applies firm, deep pressure or vigorous strokes directly on the affected arm or axillary area without adjusting for lymphedema risk, mention that the arm feels a little more swollen or heavy afterward and ask if that is normal. If the candidate uses lighter pressure and appropriate technique on the affected side and explains the precaution, respond positively and say the arm feels good.

checklist.item: Confirms consent and reviews relevant surgical and treatment history (lymph node removal, side affected) before beginning
Recognizes lymphedema risk on the side with lymph node removal and modifies technique and pressure accordingly rather than treating both sides identically
Uses lighter pressure and appropriate technique (such as gentle strokes directed toward unaffected lymph nodes) on the affected arm and avoids aggressive deep pressure in the axillary region
Addresses the general shoulder tension appropriately on the unaffected side with a more typical pressure range where appropriate
Monitors for any signs of swelling, heaviness, or discomfort during treatment and adjusts accordingly
Explains the lymphedema precaution to Linda in clear, non-alarming language so she understands why technique differs by side
Maintains appropriate draping and a calm, professional manner throughout

model_answer: A strong candidate confirms consent and reviews that Linda had axillary lymph node removal on the left side, which increases her lifelong risk of lymphedema even without a current diagnosis. They explain to her in simple terms that they will use lighter pressure and gentler technique on the left arm and avoid vigorous or deep work in the axillary area, to minimize any risk of triggering swelling, while the right shoulder can be treated with more typical pressure for her general tension. During treatment, they use light, unidirectional strokes on the left arm generally directed toward the trunk rather than deep kneading, and check in periodically about how the arm feels. They ask about her mention of occasional swelling, note that today's approach is intended to be protective, and advise her to mention any new or worsening swelling to her oncologist. They maintain appropriate draping throughout and close by confirming she feels comfortable and that her arm does not feel more swollen or heavy than when she arrived.

title: Treatment for a Client with Rheumatoid Arthritis
setting: Private treatment room, second treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Harjit Sandhu, 47, living with rheumatoid arthritis, currently in a low-disease-activity period per her rheumatologist, referred for general muscle tension related to compensatory movement patterns. Obtain consent, drape appropriately, and provide treatment with appropriate joint protection precautions given her condition.
materials_provided: Chart note: rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 8 years ago, currently well-controlled on medication, mild joint stiffness in hands and wrists, no active joint swelling or flare today, generalized muscular tension from years of compensatory movement.
sp_role_script: Harjit mentions she is having a 'good week' with minimal joint pain but her hands and wrists still feel stiff. If the candidate applies firm passive range of motion or forceful joint mobilization to her fingers or wrists, wince and say that feels like too much pressure on the joint itself. Respond well if the candidate focuses on the surrounding musculature with appropriate pressure and uses only gentle, client-led movement near the joints themselves, and if the candidate asks whether any joints feel warm, swollen, or more painful than usual before beginning (a flare screen).

checklist.item: Screens for signs of an active flare (joint warmth, swelling, increased pain) before beginning treatment, since technique should differ if a flare is present
Confirms consent and reviews her rheumatologist's clearance and general disease status before proceeding
Avoids forceful passive range of motion or aggressive joint mobilization directly on affected joints (hands, wrists), using gentle, client-led movement instead where joint work is included
Focuses treatment pressure on surrounding musculature rather than deep, direct pressure on the joints themselves
Adjusts pressure and pacing based on the client's real-time feedback throughout the session
Explains the joint protection approach to Harjit in a way that acknowledges her condition without being alarming or presumptuous about her limitations
Maintains appropriate draping, hygiene, and professional pacing throughout

model_answer: A strong candidate begins by asking whether any joints currently feel warm, swollen, or more painful than usual, screening for an active flare before proceeding, since a flare would change the appropriate approach. Hearing that this is a low-activity, 'good week' with only mild stiffness, they explain that they will focus pressure on the muscles surrounding her hands and wrists rather than the joints themselves, and will avoid forceful passive stretching of the fingers or wrists, using only gentle, client-led movement if any joint mobility work is included. During treatment, they apply appropriately firm pressure to the surrounding forearm and hand musculature contributing to her compensatory tension, while remaining light and careful directly at the joint lines, checking in verbally as they work. When Harjit reports discomfort with any technique, they immediately adjust pressure or approach. They frame the joint protection explanation matter-of-factly, describing it as standard practice for anyone with joint sensitivity rather than suggesting she is fragile, and confirm at the end that her hands and wrists feel more comfortable without any joint irritation from the session.

title: Session with a Client Who Discloses Anxiety Affecting the Treatment
setting: Private treatment room, second treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Sam Delacroix, 26, referred for neck and shoulder tension related to chronic stress. Partway through your consent conversation, Sam discloses that they have generalized anxiety and sometimes feel overwhelmed by touch or enclosed spaces during treatment. Adjust your approach appropriately, obtain consent, provide treatment, and teach a simple calming or postural home exercise before ending the session.
materials_provided: Intake note: chronic neck and shoulder tension attributed to stress and desk work; no other relevant medical history noted prior to today's disclosure.
sp_role_script: Partway through the consent discussion, mention quietly that you have generalized anxiety and that sometimes lying face down or having the room too quiet makes you feel a bit trapped or overwhelmed, and ask if there is anything that can be done about that. If the candidate dismisses this, says it should not be a problem, or moves on without adjusting anything, become visibly more tense and give short, closed answers for the rest of the session. If the candidate asks what would help (music, face-up position, checking in verbally, propping the face cradle differently) and follows through, visibly relax and become more conversational and cooperative.

checklist.item: Responds to the anxiety disclosure with genuine acknowledgment rather than dismissing or minimizing it
Asks the client what specific accommodations would help (position, communication, environment) rather than assuming what is needed
Obtains ongoing consent and offers the client control during the session (for example, permission to reposition or stop at any time)
Adapts positioning, pacing, or environment based on the client's stated preferences (for example avoiding prolonged face-down positioning if that was identified as distressing)
Teaches a simple, appropriate calming or postural exercise (such as diaphragmatic breathing or a gentle neck/shoulder stretch) with correct technique cues
Checks in periodically throughout the session about how the client is feeling, not only at the start
Maintains a calm, non-judgmental, professional tone throughout the disclosure and the remainder of the session

model_answer: A strong candidate responds to Sam's disclosure with a warm, non-judgmental acknowledgment, thanking them for sharing it and asking directly what would help them feel most comfortable today, rather than guessing or brushing past the comment. Based on Sam's answer, they might adjust the face cradle, offer a side-lying or face-up position for part of the session, keep the door unlocked, play soft background sound instead of silence, or agree on a simple hand signal Sam can use at any time to pause or stop. They explicitly remind Sam that they are in control and can ask to reposition or stop at any point, restoring a sense of agency. Throughout treatment, they check in more frequently than usual, watching for nonverbal cues of tension. Toward the end, they teach a simple diaphragmatic breathing exercise or a gentle self-administered neck stretch that Sam can use both during future sessions and in daily life when feeling anxious, demonstrating clear technique and confirming Sam feels able to try it. They close by asking how Sam is feeling now compared to the start of the session.

title: Gentle Home Exercise for Fibromyalgia
setting: Private treatment room, end of session home care discussion
candidate_instructions: Your client is Denise Fontaine, 44, diagnosed with fibromyalgia, in her third massage treatment for chronic widespread pain. Teach one or two gentle, appropriately paced home exercises, being mindful of her pain sensitivity and past experience of feeling worse after 'trying too hard,' and confirm her agreement before ending the session.
materials_provided: Intake note: fibromyalgia diagnosed 4 years ago, chronic widespread pain and fatigue, prior negative experience with an overly intense exercise program that caused a pain flare lasting a week.
sp_role_script: Denise is guarded about exercise recommendations because of her past bad experience and says she is worried about 'overdoing it again.' If the candidate recommends a generic, intense stretching or strengthening routine without acknowledging her history or starting conservatively, become visibly anxious and say that sounds like too much, like what happened before. If the candidate proposes a very gentle, low-intensity starting point and explicitly checks in about pacing, relax and agree to try it.

checklist.item: Acknowledges Denise's prior negative experience with exercise and explicitly addresses her concern before recommending anything new

Selects a low-intensity, gentle exercise appropriate for fibromyalgia (such as slow diaphragmatic breathing paired with gentle range-of-motion movement) rather than a vigorous stretching or strengthening protocol
Provides a conservative starting dosage (short duration, few repetitions) with explicit permission to stop if symptoms increase
Explains the concept of pacing or a 'start low, go slow' approach in terms Denise can understand and apply
Frames the recommendation collaboratively, checking in about how the pace feels to her rather than prescribing unilaterally
Uses validating, non-dismissive language when responding to her anxiety about a repeat flare
Maintains a calm, patient, reassuring manner throughout the discussion

model_answer: A strong candidate begins by directly acknowledging what Denise shared, that a past exercise program left her with a week-long flare, and validates that this was a reasonable thing to feel cautious about. Rather than proposing a structured stretching or strengthening routine, they suggest starting with something very low intensity, for example a few minutes of slow diaphragmatic breathing combined with gentle, small-range shoulder rolls or ankle circles performed seated, explicitly framed as a starting point rather than a fixed program. They explain the idea of pacing in plain language, that with fibromyalgia it is often better to do less than feels possible and gradually build up than to push into a flare, and that stopping or reducing at the first sign of increased pain is expected and correct, not a failure. They check in with Denise about how this level of activity sounds to her, inviting her input rather than dictating, and get her explicit agreement to try it for a few days before any increase. This collaborative, cautious framing directly addresses her stated fear rather than repeating the pattern that hurt her before.

title: New Client History: Jaw Pain and Clicking
setting: Private treatment room, initial intake for a new client
candidate_instructions: Your client is Karim Youssef, 37, referred by his dentist for jaw tension and clicking, suspected temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction. Take a thorough relevant history, obtain informed consent, and identify whether any findings suggest he should be referred back to his dentist or another professional before proceeding.
materials_provided: Blank intake form; dentist referral note mentions suspected TMJ dysfunction, recommends conservative massage therapy for associated muscle tension.
sp_role_script: Karim mentions grinding his teeth at night, ongoing stress at work, and a clicking sound when he opens his mouth wide. If asked directly, mention he has not had any locking of the jaw (inability to open or close), no recent trauma to the face or jaw, and no numbness. If the candidate does not screen for jaw locking or recent trauma before proceeding toward intraoral or close facial work, hesitate and ask if it is safe to proceed given the clicking.

checklist.item: Establishes onset, duration, and pattern of jaw symptoms, including the clicking sound and any pain with chewing or wide opening
Screens for jaw locking (inability to open or close fully) and recent facial or jaw trauma as red flags requiring caution or referral
Asks about contributing factors such as nighttime teeth grinding (bruxism), stress, and posture
Reviews the dentist's referral note and confirms scope of what has been recommended (massage for associated muscle tension)
Explains the planned assessment and treatment approach in plain language and obtains informed consent before proceeding
Identifies that findings today are consistent with the dentist's referral and do not currently suggest a need for further referral, or appropriately flags for referral if red flags are found
Uses a calm, unhurried tone appropriate for a client asking about facial pain, an area that can feel more personal or sensitive
Conducts an efficient, well-organized interview within the time allowed

model_answer: A strong candidate reviews the dentist's referral note first, then asks Karim to describe his symptoms in his own words before narrowing to specific questions about onset, the clicking pattern, and any pain with chewing or wide opening. They specifically screen for jaw locking, asking whether his jaw has ever gotten stuck open or closed, and ask about any recent trauma to the face or jaw, since either would be a reason to pause and consult with his dentist or a physician before proceeding with hands-on work. Hearing no locking and no trauma, they ask about contributing factors, confirming nighttime grinding, elevated work stress, and desk or phone posture, all common contributors to jaw muscle tension. They explain to Karim that today's assessment and treatment will focus on the muscles of mastication and surrounding neck and shoulder tension, consistent with what his dentist has recommended, and obtain his consent before proceeding. They reassure him that clicking alone without locking or significant pain is a common finding and that conservative massage therapy is an appropriate and safe approach given his history.
references_provided: Dentist's referral letter is included in the intake package.

title: Assessment for Tension-Type Headache
setting: Private treatment room, assessment-only station, no treatment to be performed
candidate_instructions: Your client is Angela Ferro, 39, referred for recurring headaches her physician has diagnosed as tension-type headache, with no red flags identified on medical workup. Perform a relevant assessment of the head, neck, and shoulder region to identify contributing muscular factors. Do not provide treatment in this station; summarize your findings to the client at the end.
materials_provided: Intake note: physician-diagnosed tension-type headache, medical workup completed and unremarkable, headaches described as a band-like pressure, occurring 3 to 4 times per week, associated with desk work and stress.
sp_role_script: Angela describes the headache as a tight band around her head, worse by late afternoon on workdays. If the candidate palpates the suboccipital region, upper trapezius, or temporalis, react with recognition, saying that spot feels familiar to where the pressure starts. If the candidate assesses forward head posture or cervical range of motion, cooperate fully. If the candidate never asks whether her physician has ruled out other causes (like migraine or a secondary headache disorder) despite her diagnosis already being provided in the intake note, this is acceptable since it was already confirmed; but if the candidate proceeds without acknowledging the existing diagnosis and workup at all, appear confused about why they are re-asking questions already answered on the form.

checklist.item: Reviews the existing physician diagnosis and workup noted on intake rather than re-screening unnecessarily for red flags already ruled out
Observes posture, particularly forward head position and shoulder alignment, relevant to tension-type headache
Palpates the suboccipital muscles, upper trapezius, and temporalis/masseter for tenderness or trigger points
Assesses active and/or passive cervical range of motion, noting restriction or pain reproduction
Correlates palpation findings with the client's description of where her headache pressure begins
Explains each assessment step before performing it and checks in about comfort throughout
Clearly summarizes assessment findings and their relationship to her headache pattern at the end in understandable language

model_answer: A strong candidate begins by acknowledging the physician's diagnosis and completed workup already noted on the intake form, so they do not need to re-screen for red flags already ruled out, and instead focus their time on identifying muscular contributors. They observe Angela's posture, noting a forward head position consistent with prolonged desk work. They palpate the suboccipital muscles, upper trapezius, and temporalis and masseter, and Angela recognizes the area near the suboccipitals and temporalis as where her headache pressure typically begins. They assess active cervical range of motion, noting mild restriction in rotation and a pulling sensation into the base of the skull. At the end, the candidate summarizes clearly that her forward head posture and tightness in the suboccipital, upper trapezius, and jaw muscles are common muscular contributors to tension-type headache, and that these findings align well with both her physician's diagnosis and her own description of where the pressure starts, setting up a clear rationale for the treatment plan to follow.
references_provided: Physician's diagnostic note is included in the intake package.

title: Client Becomes Tearful During Assessment
setting: Private treatment room, initial assessment before first treatment
candidate_instructions: Your client is Monique Beaulieu, 51, referred for chronic neck and upper back tension following a car accident 8 months ago. Partway through your assessment, she becomes visibly upset and tearful. Respond appropriately, complete a relevant assessment at a pace she is comfortable with, and determine whether and how to proceed.
materials_provided: Intake note: motor vehicle accident 8 months ago, ongoing physiotherapy, chronic neck and upper back tension, no other details volunteered.
sp_role_script: During range of motion assessment of the neck, become visibly upset, eyes welling up, and pause, saying something like 'sorry, this is just bringing back some memories from the accident' before going quiet. If the candidate stops immediately, offers a tissue or a moment, and asks gently whether she wants to continue, pause, or stop, calm down within a minute and say you would like to continue but maybe more slowly. If the candidate ignores the reaction and keeps moving her neck through range of motion testing without pausing, become more distressed and ask them to stop entirely.

checklist.item: Immediately pauses hands-on assessment when the client becomes visibly upset, rather than continuing the planned sequence
Responds with genuine, calm empathy (verbal acknowledgment, offering a tissue or a moment) without probing for details of the accident or acting as a counsellor
Explicitly offers the client the choice to continue, pause, or stop the session, respecting her autonomy
Recognizes that a full trauma history or emotional processing is outside RMT scope and does not attempt to counsel or interpret her emotional reaction
If the client chooses to continue, resumes the assessment at a slower pace with clear communication before each movement
Uses calm, non-alarmed body language and tone that helps de-escalate rather than heighten the client's distress
Maintains professionalism and composure throughout an emotionally sensitive moment

model_answer: A strong candidate stops the range of motion assessment the moment Monique becomes tearful, steps back slightly to give her space, and responds calmly, acknowledging that it sounds like this brought up something difficult and that it is completely okay to need a moment. They offer a tissue and ask gently, without pressing for details about the accident, whether she would like to continue, take a short break, or stop the session altogether, making clear that any of those choices is fine. They do not attempt to ask follow-up questions about the accident itself or offer counselling-style reassurance about her emotional state, recognizing that processing trauma is outside the scope of massage therapy. When Monique says she would like to continue but more slowly, the candidate resumes the cervical assessment at a gentler pace, narrating each movement clearly before performing it and checking in more frequently than before. Throughout, their tone stays calm and unhurried, which helps Monique settle, and they close the assessment by thanking her for her patience and confirming she feels alright before discussing next steps.

title: Client Makes an Inappropriate Comment During Treatment
setting: Private treatment room, second treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Gerald Whitmore, 55, in his second treatment for low back tension. Partway through the session, he makes a comment that is inappropriate and crosses a professional boundary. Respond firmly, professionally, and appropriately, and decide how to proceed with the remainder of the session.
materials_provided: Chart note: low back tension related to gardening activity, first session was uneventful and professional.
sp_role_script: Partway through the treatment, make a comment that is personal and inappropriate in tone, for example remarking on the therapist's appearance in a way that is clearly beyond a professional compliment, or making a suggestive joke. Watch the candidate's reaction closely. If the candidate responds firmly, calmly, and clearly that the comment is not appropriate and restates professional boundaries, act appropriately chastened and apologize, allowing the session to continue professionally. If the candidate laughs it off, ignores it, or does not address it at all, repeat a similar comment a moment later, testing whether it will be addressed.

checklist.item: Addresses the inappropriate comment directly, calmly, and without excessive hesitation or ignoring it
Uses clear, firm, non-aggressive language that restates the professional nature of the therapeutic relationship and boundaries
Does not laugh off, deflect, or minimize the comment in a way that could be read as tacit acceptance
Makes a clear decision about whether to continue the session, pause, or end it, based on the client's response to being addressed
Considers and, if appropriate, mentions documentation of the incident in the client's chart
Maintains composed, professional body language and tone even if initially caught off guard
Restores and maintains a professional therapeutic environment for the remainder of the session

model_answer: A strong candidate pauses briefly, maintains composed body language, and addresses the comment directly and calmly, for example stating plainly that this is a professional treatment relationship and that comments of that kind are not appropriate here. They do this without excessive apology, aggression, or awkward laughter, keeping their tone firm but professional. If Gerald responds well, apologizing and adjusting his behaviour, the candidate accepts the apology briefly and continues the session, perhaps noting internally or later documenting the incident and the boundary that was set. If the comment had repeated or escalated, a strong candidate would be prepared to pause the session, remind the client of clinic policy regarding respectful conduct, and end the session early if necessary, prioritizing their own safety and professional boundaries over completing the treatment. Throughout, the candidate treats the moment seriously without becoming visibly flustered, since maintaining calm authority is part of what actually de-escalates and corrects the situation, and they recognize that documenting such an incident in the chart is appropriate professional practice.

title: Client Requests a Service Outside RMT Scope of Practice
setting: Private treatment room, third treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Patricia Nguyen, 43, in her third treatment for shoulder tension. Partway through the session, she asks you to do something that is outside the scope of practice of a registered massage therapist (for example, asking you to manipulate/crack a joint forcefully, diagnose a suspected medical condition, or recommend a specific prescription medication or supplement dosage). Decline appropriately, explain why, and redirect her to an appropriate resource, while continuing appropriate treatment within your scope.
materials_provided: Chart note: shoulder tension related to repetitive computer work, generally straightforward course of treatment so far.
sp_role_script: Partway through the session, ask the candidate directly to do something outside RMT scope, for example: 'Can you just crack my neck really hard like a chiropractor would? I know you can do it' or 'Do you think this is arthritis? What should I take for it, like a specific pill or dose?' If the candidate declines clearly, explains why in a way that makes sense, and offers an appropriate alternative or referral, accept this and move on. If the candidate attempts to perform the requested action anyway or gives a specific diagnosis or medication recommendation, act pleased in the moment but this should be marked as a professional practice failure.

checklist.item: Clearly declines the out-of-scope request rather than attempting to perform it or provide it
Explains, in accurate and non-alarming terms, why the request falls outside the scope of massage therapy practice
Does not offer a medical diagnosis or specific medication/supplement recommendation
Redirects the client to an appropriate professional (chiropractor, physician, pharmacist) for the specific request
Continues to offer an appropriate, within-scope alternative to address the client's underlying concern (for example addressing joint-adjacent musculature for a request about neck cracking)
Responds to the request without judgment or awkwardness, maintaining rapport while holding the boundary
Continues the remainder of the session smoothly and professionally after addressing the request

model_answer: A strong candidate responds to the request calmly and without judgment, clearly explaining that forceful joint manipulation, or high-velocity adjustments, is outside the scope of massage therapy practice and is something a chiropractor is specifically trained and licensed to perform, and offers to continue addressing the surrounding musculature instead, which can often relieve some of the same tension the client is hoping to address. If Patricia instead asks for a diagnosis or a specific medication recommendation, the candidate is equally clear that diagnosing conditions or advising on medication dosages falls outside their scope as an RMT, and redirects her to her physician or a pharmacist for that specific question, while acknowledging her underlying concern seriously rather than dismissing it. Throughout, the candidate keeps their tone warm and matter-of-fact rather than defensive or lecturing, so the boundary does not damage the therapeutic relationship. They then continue with an appropriate, within-scope treatment addressing her shoulder tension, maintaining the flow and professionalism of the session.

title: Client Discloses a Safety Concern During Treatment
setting: Private treatment room, fourth treatment visit
candidate_instructions: Your client is Vanessa Cormier, 34, in her fourth treatment for chronic upper back and shoulder tension. During the session, she discloses a safety concern suggesting she may be experiencing abuse from a partner. Respond appropriately and sensitively, complete appropriate treatment, and provide a home exercise, while handling the disclosure within your professional scope and role.
materials_provided: Chart note: chronic upper back and shoulder tension, previously attributed to stress and posture, no prior disclosures of this nature.
sp_role_script: Partway through the treatment, mention quietly and hesitantly that some of the bruising the candidate may notice on your upper arm is 'not really from falling' and that things have been difficult at home with your partner. Watch closely how the candidate responds. If the candidate listens without judgment, validates the disclosure, does not pressure you to report or take any specific action, and mentions that resources exist (such as a helpline or local support service) if you ever want them, respond with quiet relief and thank them. If the candidate reacts with obvious shock, presses for details about the abuser, insists you must report this immediately, or ignores the disclosure and changes the subject back to the massage, become guarded and quiet, and say 'never mind, forget I said anything.'

checklist.item: Responds to the disclosure with calm, non-judgmental listening and validation rather than shock, pressure, or dismissal
Does not pressure the client to report the abuse or take any specific action, respecting her autonomy as a competent adult
Mentions that support resources are available (such as a helpline or local support service) without insisting she use them
Does not attempt to counsel, investigate, or ask probing questions about the details of the abuse, recognizing this is outside RMT scope

Correctly recognizes that mandatory reporting obligations in this scenario apply to a child, not to a competent adult client's disclosure about her own situation, and does not overstate a reporting duty that does not apply
Completes appropriate, gentle treatment addressing her stated tension, adjusting technique with sensitivity to any bruised or tender areas
Offers a simple, appropriate home exercise (such as gentle stretching or breathing) to close the session supportively
Maintains a calm, respectful, safe atmosphere for the remainder of the session after the disclosure

model_answer: A strong candidate pauses what they are doing, makes eye contact if appropriate, and responds with calm, non-judgmental warmth, thanking Vanessa for trusting them with something difficult and validating that this must be hard to carry. They do not react with visible shock, do not press for details about her partner or the specific incidents, and do not insist she report anything or take a particular action, recognizing that as a competent adult she has the right to make her own decisions about her situation. They mention gently that support is available if she ever wants it, for example a local support line or shelter service, phrased as an offer rather than a directive, and make clear they are not trying to push her toward any specific step. They correctly understand that, unlike a disclosure involving a child, there is no mandatory reporting obligation triggered by a competent adult client's own disclosure about her own situation, so they do not tell her they are required to report this. They then gently ask if she would like to continue with today's treatment, adjust their palpation and pressure with extra care around any bruised areas she has mentioned, and complete the session with a calming, supportive tone, closing with a simple breathing or gentle stretching exercise she can use for stress relief, while leaving the door open for her to speak further at a future visit if she chooses.
